questions.title: Vessels with valves
questions.question: Which of these vessels have valves?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Arteries carry blood under high pulsatile pressure away from the heart and do not need valves; only veins, the low-pressure return side, have them.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Arterioles, like arteries, are on the high-pressure outflow side and have no valves; venules are too small and numerous to be a standard teaching pairing here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capillaries are single-cell-thick exchange vessels with no muscular wall and no valves.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Veins do have valves, but capillaries do not, so this pairing is wrong.
explanations.E: Correct. Both veins and lymphatic vessels carry fluid against gravity back toward the heart at low pressure, and both rely on multiple one-way valves, together with surrounding skeletal muscle contraction, to keep that flow moving in a single direction. Arteries and capillaries, by contrast, have no valves because they do not need to prevent backflow in the same way. This shared low-pressure, one-directional design is why veins and lymphatics are grouped together for this fact.

questions.learning_objective: State that lymphatic vessels, like veins, have valves to keep flow unidirectional.

questions.title: Area without lymphatic vessels
questions.question: What area does NOT have lymphatic vessels?

explanations.A: Correct. Lymphatic vessels are absent from a small set of avascular or immune-privileged tissues, including the teeth, cartilage, the central nervous system and bone marrow. The upper limb, foot and abdomen all have well developed lymphatic drainage as part of the whole-body lymphatic network. The teeth, being hard, largely avascular structures, are one of the standard exceptions taught alongside cartilage and the eye's cornea.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The upper limb has a rich lymphatic network draining ultimately to the axillary lymph nodes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The foot has lymphatic vessels draining toward the popliteal and then inguinal lymph nodes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The abdomen has extensive lymphatic drainage, including the mesenteric and aortic (para-aortic) node groups.
explanations.E: Incorrect. "Peripheral nervous system" is not one of the standard avascular exceptions taught for this fact; the exception is the central nervous system, not the peripheral nerves.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the teeth as a site lacking lymphatic vessels.

questions.title: Tonsils versus lymphoid organs
questions.question: What differentiates tonsils from lymphoid organs?

options.B: Tonsils do not have a capsule.
options.D: Tonsils are responsible for T cell maturation.
options.E: Tonsils are grouped in different body regions (cervical, axillary, inguinal).

explanations.A: Incorrect. This states the opposite of the true distinguishing feature; a true lymphoid organ has a capsule, and the tonsils do not.
explanations.B: Correct. Lymphoid tissue is divided into encapsulated lymphoid organs, such as lymph nodes, the spleen and the thymus, and unencapsulated (diffuse) lymphoid tissue, such as the tonsils and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT). The tonsils are collections of lymphoid tissue that lack a surrounding fibrous capsule, which is exactly why they are classed as lymphoid tissue rather than a true lymphoid organ. This capsule/no-capsule distinction is the standard teaching line dividing the two categories.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Breaking down old red blood cells is a spleen function, not a feature that distinguishes tonsils from lymphoid organs.
explanations.D: Incorrect. T cell maturation is a thymus function, not a tonsil feature, and does not address the capsule distinction being asked about.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Grouping by body region describes lymph nodes generally (cervical, axillary, inguinal, and so on), not a feature specific to tonsils.

questions.learning_objective: State that tonsils lack a capsule, unlike true lymphoid organs.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.58

questions.title: Lymphoid organ shrinking with puberty
questions.question: What lymphoid organ decreases in size with puberty?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tonsils are largest in mid-childhood and shrink somewhat with age, but they are not the organ classically taught for puberty-onset involution.
explanations.B: Correct. The thymus is large and highly active in fetal life and childhood, when it drives T-lymphocyte maturation, and then undergoes progressive involution beginning around puberty, with lymphoid tissue gradually being replaced by fat. This age-related shrinkage is a classic teaching point distinguishing the thymus from other lymphoid organs, which do not show the same puberty-linked involution pattern. By adulthood the thymus is a small fraction of its childhood size.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The spleen does not undergo a puberty-linked involution; it remains functionally active as a blood filter and immune organ throughout adult life.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) is distributed diffusely and is not the organ classically taught for puberty-related involution.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lymph nodes remain active immune filtering stations throughout life and are not described as involuting at puberty.

questions.learning_objective: State that the thymus decreases in size (involutes) from puberty onward.

questions.title: Lymph capillaries joining
questions.question: Lymph capillaries join to form….....

explanations.A: Correct. Lymph begins in blind-ended lymphatic capillaries within tissues, which unite with one another to form progressively larger lymphatic vessels. Those lymphatic vessels, after passing through one or more lymph nodes for filtering, unite in turn to form larger lymph trunks, which finally drain into one of the two large lymphatic ducts (thoracic duct or right lymphatic duct). Lymph capillaries are therefore the first step in this chain, joining directly to form lymph vessels, not trunks, nodes or ducts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Lymph trunks are formed further along the chain, by the union of multiple lymph vessels, not directly from capillaries.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lymph nodes are filtering stations that lymphatic vessels pass through, not structures formed by capillaries joining together.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lymph ducts (thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct) are the final, largest structures in the chain, formed by the union of lymph trunks, not directly from capillaries.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The thoracic duct is the single largest lymphatic vessel in the body, the end point of the whole collecting chain, not the immediate product of capillaries joining.

questions.learning_objective: State that lymph capillaries unite to form lymph vessels, the first step in the lymphatic collecting chain.

questions.title: Right upper limb lymphatic drainage
questions.question: The right upper limb drains its lymph in ……………

explanations.A: Incorrect. The thoracic duct drains lymph from the whole body below the diaphragm and from the left side of the head, neck, thorax and left upper limb, not the right upper limb.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The superior vena cava is a blood vessel that receives venous blood, not a lymphatic collecting structure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The right internal jugular vein carries venous blood from the head and neck; it is where the right lymphatic duct ultimately empties, but it is not itself the lymph trunk draining the upper limb.
explanations.D: Correct. Lymph from the right upper limb, together with lymph from the right side of the head/neck and right thorax, drains into the right lymphatic duct (or directly into the right subclavian/jugular venous confluence via separate trunks including the right subclavian lymph trunk). This right-sided drainage is confined to the right side of the body, in contrast to the much larger thoracic duct, which drains everywhere else. The right lymph trunk is therefore the correct destination named among these options for right upper limb lymph.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The right atrium receives venous blood returning to the heart; lymph enters the venous system further upstream, at the great veins of the neck, not directly into the heart.

questions.learning_objective: State that the right upper limb drains its lymph into the right lymph trunk.

questions.title: Largest lymphatic vessel
questions.question: Which of the following is largest lymphatic vessel in the body?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right lymphatic duct is a short vessel draining only the right upper quadrant of the body, considerably smaller than the thoracic duct.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no separate "left lymphatic duct" as a standard named structure; the left side of the body drains via the thoracic duct itself.
explanations.C: Correct. The thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body, collecting lymph from both lower limbs, the abdomen and pelvis, the left side of the thorax, and the left side of the head, neck and upper limb, before emptying into the venous system at the left venous angle (junction of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins). Its wide collecting territory, roughly three-quarters of the body, is why it dwarfs the much smaller right lymphatic duct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior vena cava is a large blood vein, not a lymphatic vessel.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava is likewise a large blood vein, not a lymphatic vessel.

questions.learning_objective: State that the thoracic duct is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.58

questions.title: Lymphoid tissue that is not a lymphoid organ
questions.question: Which of the following is considered lymphoid tissue not lymphoid organ?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The spleen is an encapsulated lymphoid organ, not diffuse lymphoid tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The thymus gland is an encapsulated lymphoid organ.
explanations.C: Correct. Lymphoid tissue is split into true, encapsulated lymphoid organs (lymph nodes, spleen, thymus) and diffuse, unencapsulated lymphoid tissue such as the tonsils and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue. The tonsils lack the fibrous capsule that defines a true lymphoid organ, which is why they are classified as lymphoid tissue rather than a lymphoid organ, the same distinction tested by this lecture's capsule question. This classification restates the same capsule-based rule from a different angle, asking which option is the tissue rather than the organ.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An axillary lymph node is a true, encapsulated lymphoid organ.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An inguinal lymph node is likewise a true, encapsulated lymphoid organ.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the tonsils as lymphoid tissue rather than a true (encapsulated) lymphoid organ.

questions.title: Pelvic lymphatic collection
questions.question: Lymphatics from the pelvis are collected by which of the following lymphatic ducts?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The right lymphatic duct drains only the right upper quadrant of the body (right side of head/neck, right upper limb, right thorax), not the pelvis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. There is no separate "left lymphatic duct"; the left side and the lower body both drain via the thoracic duct.
explanations.C: Correct. The thoracic duct begins in the abdomen as the cisterna chyli, which receives lymph from both lower limbs and the pelvis via the paired lumbar lymph trunks, together with intestinal lymph. It then ascends through the thorax to empty into the venous system at the left venous angle. Pelvic lymphatics are therefore collected by the thoracic duct, consistent with the thoracic duct's role as the drainage route for everywhere below the diaphragm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The superior vena cava is a blood vein, not a lymphatic collecting duct.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The inferior vena cava is a blood vein, not a lymphatic collecting duct, even though it also drains the pelvis's venous blood.

questions.learning_objective: State that pelvic lymphatics are collected by the thoracic duct via the cisterna chyli and lumbar trunks.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer letter in right-margin column, p.58

questions.title: Structure without lymphatic vessels
questions.question: Which of the following structures does not contain lymphatic vessels?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The liver has a rich lymphatic drainage, producing a large proportion of the body's total lymph flow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The kidney has lymphatic vessels draining toward the lateral aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes.
explanations.C: Correct. The central nervous system, including the brain, has no conventional lymphatic vessels; instead it relies on the blood-brain barrier and, more recently described, the glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic systems for fluid clearance, distinct from the classical lymphatic vessels found elsewhere in the body. This is the same avascular/lymphatic-free exception category as the teeth and cartilage, tested earlier in this same lecture. The brain is therefore the standard answer among solid organs for a structure lacking conventional lymphatic vessels.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The small intestine has an extensive lymphatic network, including specialised lacteals that absorb dietary fat, draining to the mesenteric lymph nodes.

questions.learning_objective: State that the brain (CNS) lacks conventional lymphatic vessels.

questions.title: First lymph node group to examine in breast cancer
questions.question: If your patient is diagnosed to have breast cancer, you should firstly examine which of the following lymph node groups?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The aortic (para-aortic) nodes drain abdominal and pelvic structures, not the breast.
explanations.B: Correct. The breast's lymphatic drainage is predominantly (around three-quarters) to the axillary lymph nodes, with the remainder draining to parasternal (internal thoracic) nodes and a small amount to nodes of the opposite breast and the abdominal wall. Because breast cancer spreads first through this lymphatic route, the axillary nodes are the first group examined clinically and are staged surgically (sentinel node biopsy or axillary clearance) to guide treatment. This makes axillary lymph node examination the standard first step in a breast cancer work-up.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The iliac nodes drain pelvic structures, not the breast.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The inguinal nodes drain the lower limb, perineum and lower anal canal, not the breast.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The popliteal nodes drain the leg and foot, not the breast.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axillary lymph nodes are the first group examined in suspected breast cancer, as the breast's main lymphatic drainage route.
